articles.title: ‘Like a tired boxer, battered by applause’: as Andrew Scott’s biopic premieres, Richard Eyre remembers Ian Charleson’s superb, near-death Hamlet
articles.summary: In 1989, the Chariots of Fire actor took on the incredible task of playing Shakespeare’s prince while terminally ill from Aids. This weekend sees the world premiere of Elsinore, a new film about the episode, itself heavily-tipped for awards.
body: Ian Charleson was one of the finest actors of his generation and an important figure in the fight for gay rights. Yet the extraordinary circumstances of his final performance as Hamlet, just months before his death, are less familiar.

Now, a new film is bringing that haunting production back to life. Elsinore, directed by Simon Stone and starring Andrew Scott as the Scottish actor, will premiere at Telluride this weekend before opening the London film festival in October.

Charleson was 40 and terminally ill with Aids when he was cast as Hamlet in Richard Eyre’s 1989 production at the National Theatre, after Daniel Day-Lewis abruptly left the role. Charleson had first played Hamlet 15 years earlier and persuaded Eyre to let him reprise it, despite the director’s misgivings about his health.
“Ian was very bright, very witty, mischievous,” Eyre told the Guardian. “He was beyond good-looking. He was beautiful, and he had a beautiful singing voice.”

articles.title: Latcho Drom director Tony Gatlif dies aged 77
articles.summary: Film-maker acclaimed for his celebrations of Roma culture had been working on a ‘historical film project’ in Provence. Tony Gatlif, the French director of more than 20 films that mostly concentrated on celebrating Roma culture across the world, has died aged 77.
body: His family said in a statement to AFP that Gatlif died on Wednesday of “a health issue” while working on a “historical film project” in Arles in Provence, France. “The beauty of his films, his generosity, his joy, his poetry, and his love of music will remain with us forever.”
The statement, from his wife, children and grandchildren wished him “ Latcho Drom ”, a Roma phrase meaning “safe journey”.

Latcho Drom is also the title of Gatlif’s breakthrough 1993 film, a celebration of Roma music that moves from India to Spain, and which won the Un Certain Regard award at the Cannes film festival that year.

Gatlif had more success in 1997 with Gadjo Dilo, which featured Romain Duris as a Frenchman who is searching for a Roma singer in Romania; it won a Silver Leopard at the Locarno film festival and a César award for best original music.

articles.title: Queer Edward II review – funny, touching time capsule of Derek Jarman at work
articles.summary: Venice film festival: Filmed during the making of his queer royal feature, while the director was living with HIV, the candid footage includes uproarious scenes at a Cliff Richard rehearsal.
body: There could hardly be a more vivid time-capsule film about the publicly funded British arts scene in the early 1990s than this engrossing fly-on-the-wall documentary about Derek Jarman and his movie Edward II. Based on the play by Christopher Marlowe, it is about the 14th-century English king and his love affair with his court favourite, Piers Gaveston, with Steven Waddington and Andrew Tiernan as the leads and Tilda Swinton as Queen Isabella.

The “outing” debate now in fact looks very dated and this is the one moment where you can sense that Jarman thinks that the OutRage! protesters got it wrong by harassing and bullying Cliff Richard; we see him assuring his own team later that Tatchell gave them a real telling off for this. (Did Tatchell actually do anything of the kind? Or is that what Jarman felt ought to have happened?) It’s an absorbing and affecting portrait of a dedicated artist at work.

articles.title: ‘Many of us in Israel live in a state of shock at the savagery’: veteran director Amos Gitai returns to Gaza
articles.summary: The writer-director once called Israel’s ‘one-man New Wave’ is in Venice with The Road to Jericho, a new and poetic attempt to highlight the plight of those in the occupied West Bank.
body: The Palestinian village of Khan al-Ahmar sits off dust-blown Highway-1, between Jerusalem and Jericho in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. At the village centre is the “school of tires”, a fragile construction of rubber, wood and adobe which is attended by around 300 Bedouin boys and girls. The Israeli authorities denied the villagers an official building permit and ruled that the entire settlement is illegal. For the past eight years the school has been operating under threat of imminent demolition, a symbol of resistance to widespread settler violence.

It is only international pressure, says the veteran Israeli writer-director Amos Gitai, that has kept the place upright and still open. “The school has become a litmus paper. It is a test of how far the international community will go [to protect the rights of the people of Khan al-Ahmar]. For once, on this issue, Europe stood up and said no.” As for the future, who can tell?

articles.title: Global Content Industry Leaders Gather to Discuss ‘Multilateralism for the Moving Image’ at France’s Lumiere Summit
articles.summary: Hollywood heavyweights and top players in content and exhibition from around the world will gather in Saint-Paul-de-Vence on Sept. 7 for the landmark Lumiere Summit that aims to explore the future of film at a time of profound change that is transforming media and entertainment.
body: The summit offers a rare opportunity for senior executives, exhibitors, producers, distributors, talent representatives, financiers and other key constituencies to gather for deep conversations about where market forces are driving consumers and commerce.

“President Macron wanted to put cinema and the moving image where they belong: at the heart of the defining debates of our time,” Bruel said. “Because what is at stake extends far beyond the screen industries. Our entire image-based civilization is at a turning point. How we create, produce, distribute, watch and pass on stories is changing profoundly, with consequences for individuals and societies alike.”

Summit organizers are emphasizing the urgency of the world community to gather to address budding opportunities and structural challenges that need to be addressed through policy, contracts and trade agreements.

The CNC has recruited Variety to serve as the Lumiere Summit’s official media partner. Variety will offer extensive coverage of the summit’s sessions, key speakers and in-depth analysis of the substance of what is discussed throughout the week.

articles.summary: Digital creator Skyelar Chase, who specializes in luxury lifestyle content and has more than 1.7 million followers on TikTok, has signed with Innovative Artists Entertainment for representation in all areas.
body: The Korean American creator has “become a go-to source for all things luxury and is quickly becoming a leading tastemaker,” according to Innovative Artists. Based in New York City, Chase is currently enrolled as a student at Columbia University studying film.

Across TikTok, Instagram and YouTube, Chase has built an audience of over 2.5 million followers. According to Innovative Artists, her “consistently polished aesthetic, personal style and aspirational yet relatable content includes taking her global audience behind the scenes at major industry events like global fashion weeks and high fashion house engagements.”

Chase has been tapped by publications like InStyle and Who What Wear for exclusive coverage about her insider access at fashion week shows. In addition, she has partnered with luxury brands such as Miu Miu, Fendi, Tiffany & Co., Prada, Valentino Beauty, Dior Beauty, Dolce & Gabbana Beauty and L’Oréal Paris.

articles.title: Lea Salonga on ‘Miss Saigon,’ ‘Aladdin’ and Supporting Her Trans Son Amid Anti-Trans Rhetoric: ‘It Makes Me Intensely Afraid and Not Just for My Child’
articles.summary: Tony winner Lea Salonga admits she never really thought about getting a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. “Most of my work is in musical theater,” says Salonga, who earned international recognition for originating the role of Kim in “Miss Saigon” in 1989.
body: The Tony winner will receive a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on Sept. 4.

While she is known as a star of the stage, Salonga has had major roles on screen, too. She was the singing voice for Princess Jasmine in “Aladdin” as well as Fa Mulan in “Mulan” and “Mulan 2.” Later this month, Salonga, who made her singing debut when she was just seven years old in her native Manila, appears in “Forgotten Island,” DreamWorks Animation’s Philippines-set fantasy adventure about childhood friends who get trapped in the mystical world of Nakali.

“It centers on my culture,” Salonga tells me over a Zoom video call earlier this week. “It centers Philippine myth and folklore. We get to share our mythological creatures with the bigger world. I don’t think it’s something that I ever thought I would have seen.”

Salonga’s work as Kim earned her a Laurence Olivier Award and in 1991, she became the first Asian actress to win a Tony Award and the second-youngest actress to win for best performance by a leading actress in a musical.

articles.title: 'Not only did I survive, I thrived' - Meera Syal
articles.summary: The Wolverhampton-born comedian and actress shares her experiences in her new memoir.
body: Dame Meera Syal has said she "almost gave up" her career after being sexually harassed and assaulted by two "predators" within the media industry.

"I was out of work, I was homeless, sleeping on people's floors, and then these two things happened in quite quick succession," the Wolverhampton-born star said in a candid interview with BBC Asian Network's Amber Haque.
In her new memoir, Vigilauntie, which was published on Thursday, the actress shared that both incidents happened in her 20s, as she was struggling to secure a role.
Now aged 65, she has opened up about the harrowing experiences and reflected on how she overcame them to become one of the most well-known faces on British TV.

articles.title: How Oasis fans cracked the Celtic Park gigs code in chip shop video
articles.summary: Internet sleuths spotted sets of numbers in posters suggesting the map co-ordinates for Celtic's Parkhead stadium in Glasgow.
body: Oasis fans have uncovered a set of cryptic clues in a promo video from the band, suggesting that they will stage gigs at Celtic Park in Glasgow next year.
The Manchester rockers released the 23-second teaser on their social media accounts, showing two boys in what appears to be a Scottish chip shop.
Internet sleuths spotted sets of numbers in posters around the chippy which they worked out to be the map co-ordinates for Celtic's Parkhead stadium.
It has fuelled speculation that the band will be playing at the venue next year- possibly as the first date of a new tour.

articles.title: ‘A Place to Heal’ Review: An Intensely Performed French Teen Psych Ward Drama That Shifts Uneasily Between Reality and Fiction
articles.summary: Writer, director and actor Cédric Kahn immersed himself in a psychiatric facility for this Venice competition entry about a group of adolescents coping with emotional disorders.
body: Writer-director Cédric Kahn is perhaps best known outside France for helming tense, extremely bleak thrillers — Red Lights, Roberto Succo and L’Ennui — bathed in both film noir and existential angst. But he’s also tried his hand at several other genres, including a supernatural kids flick ( The Plane ), a gritty tale of rehab and religion ( The Prayer ), an engrossing courtroom drama ( The Goldman Case ) and, for his memorable second feature from 1994, a striking coming-of-age story called Too Much Happiness.

That setting is both the raison d’être of Kahn’s latest, which he co-wrote with Kahina Le Querrec after spending months immersed in an actual institution, and sometimes its Achilles heel. Scattered among nearly a dozen characters, even if a love triangle eventually emerges amid the group, the script is a tad too loose-limbed to turn into a gripping drama. But perhaps more questionable is how Kahn chose a mix of professional and amateur performers — some of them making their feature debut — to portray kids with deep psychological issues, toeing the line between fact and fiction, group therapy and an Actors Studio exercise, in a way that doesn’t always sit well.
